column1: In classical planning, what is the formal tuple defining a planning problem?
column2: (S, A, s0, G, T, C) — state space, action space, initial state, goal specification, transition function, and cost function.

column1: What is the computational complexity class of general classical planning, and what does this imply?
column2: PSPACE-complete — deciding whether a plan exists requires space polynomial in encoding size but potentially exponential time.

column1: What property must a heuristic satisfy for a planning algorithm to be admissible?
column2: The heuristic must never overestimate the true cost-to-goal (it must be a lower bound on actual cost).

column1: Distinguish 'completeness' from 'optimality' in a planning algorithm.
column2: Completeness means the planner finds a solution whenever one exists; optimality means it returns the minimum-cost plan (requires admissibility plus systematic exploration).

column1: Why does an agent without reflection degrade in real environments (open-loop control)?
column2: Because open-loop control only works under a perfectly modeled, deterministic, stationary environment; any deviation (distribution shift, latency, unexpected states) causes silent, irrecoverable degradation since there is no feedback correction.

column1: In the two-level reflective agent architecture, what are the 'meta-state' and 'meta-policy'?
column2: Meta-state (ŝ) encodes the agent's beliefs about its own performance; meta-policy (π̂) maps meta-states to a distribution over base policies (Π), forming an outer MDP layered atop the object-level MDP.

column1: What is Invariant 1 (Observability) for a well-posed reflection mechanism?
column2: The agent must have access to sufficient signal to compute a performance metric ρ from observations that distinguishes good outcomes from bad; otherwise reflection has no meaningful input (analogous to detectability in linear control theory).

column1: What is Invariant 2 (Credit Assignment) in reflection, and why is it hard for LLM-based agents?
column2: The agent must attribute an outcome to a specific action/sequence of actions; without this, learning signal is zero everywhere. In LLM agents this is hard because actions are multi-token generations and outcomes may manifest many tool calls later (temporal credit assignment problem).

column1: What is the core invariant governing integration of planning and reflection?
column2: Reflection must be grounded in the agent's own execution trace τ = {(s0,a0,r0),...,(st,at,rt)} — this trace is the empirical data against which the world model's accuracy is measured; without it reflection is mere speculation.

column1: In the planning-reflection meta-learning loop, what does the correction signal Δθ represent, and how is it computed?
column2: Δθ represents an update to the agent's learned world-model parameters θ (parameterizing T̂ and R̂); it is computed as Δθ = ∇θ L(τ, T̂θ, R̂θ), the gradient of a loss measuring discrepancy between model predictions and observed transitions from the execution trace.

column1: What does 'Consistency under introspection' require of a reflective agent's self-model?
column2: The self-model's predicted next state s' must closely match the actually executed next state s'_actual, satisfying ||s' - s'_actual|| < ε for small ε.

column1: What transport protocol and message format does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) use, and what are its three core primitives?
column2: MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or HTTP (with SSE) transport; its three primitives are Tools (model-invoked actions), Resources (contextual data the model can read), and Prompts (reusable instruction templates).
